title: A typology for inclusive mathematics education practices
abstract: Abstract This paper examines Inclusive Mathematics Education (IME) practices for students with Special Educational Needs (SEN) in upper primary and lower post‐primary settings. In response to the absence of shared conceptualisations of SEN and IME, the study adopts a conceptual research design and develops a typology grounded in analysis of existing literature. The aim was to categorise dominant forms of IME practice and to examine the SEN and inclusion contexts within which these practices are positioned. The analysis identified three principal approaches to SEN: General SEN, Specific SEN and Unidentified SEN. Two perspectives on inclusion were also identified, defined as Broad and Narrow. Across the reviewed studies, four dominant types of IME practice emerged: Teaching for Understanding, Constructivist Teaching, Differentiated Instruction and Teaching for Procedural Fluency. Each type comprised associated variants. This typology provides a foundational framework for conceptualising IME practice and highlights areas for further refinement, particularly where practices overlap or are multi‐typed.

title: The criticality of effective teacher–student relationships when working with students with dyslexia
abstract: Abstract This paper explores the critical role of teacher–student relationships in supporting learners with dyslexia, with a particular focus on mathematics. Through a mixed‐methods approach, the research included 10 participants aged 10 to 50+, each engaged in 35 one‐to‐one mathematics lessons. The research investigated how relational dynamics influence self‐belief, mindset and academic engagement. Data from pre/post exam papers, Q‐sort, interviews, drawings and reflective journals showed the damaging impact of negative teacher interactions. Ridicule, indifference or denial of dyslexia can reinforce fixed mindsets, heightened maths anxiety and reduced self‐efficacy. Conversely, positive relationships built on empathy, encouragement and trust enabled learners to reframe their self‐perceptions, develop resilience and achieve measurable gains in mathematical understanding. The findings showed that effective teaching for students with dyslexia extends far beyond content delivery. It relies on relationships that build emotional safety, show belief in students' potential and challenge negative viewpoints. It also demonstrated how the most powerful driver of success was not a specialist

title: Early identification and intervention of children with special educational needs: Views of teachers and parents
abstract: Abstract Early identification and intervention for children with special educational needs (SEN) are vital for their educational success and development. This study explores the experiences of teachers and parents about early identification and intervention for children with SEN in the Cape Coast Metropolis using a qualitative approach. Findings reveal challenges such as limited access to assessment centres, financial constraints and insufficient teacher training, while opportunities include teacher observation techniques, parental awareness and community engagement. Additionally, inadequate resources, placement difficulties and limited training hinder early intervention; yet individualised learning support and collaboration offer solutions. The study highlights the need for increased investment in assessment centres, teacher training and policy reforms while emphasising the importance of collaboration among educators, healthcare professionals and policymakers for inclusive education.

title: Issue Information
Allies or adversaries? A reflection on the relationship between case officers and parent/carers
abstract: Abstract The relationship between Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) case officers and parents/carers is central to the effective implementation of inclusive education policy, yet it is often characterised by tension, mistrust and conflicting expectations. By critically reflecting on whether SEND case officers and parents/carers function as allies working towards shared outcomes for children and young people, or as adversaries positioned within structurally oppositional roles, we can begin to address the areas of tension. Drawing on practitioner reflection, policy analysis and existing literature on collaborative practice, power dynamics and advocacy within statutory assessment processes, we can explore how systemic pressures, such as resource constraints, legislative frameworks and accountability measures, shape interactions and perceptions on both sides. This critical discussion highlights the tensions illustrated in the literature and uses theoretical frameworks as a useful lens to understand the SEND case officer role. Reframing the relationship from compliance‐driven negotiation to co‐produced partnership is essential for improving outcomes for children and youn

title: Before you mark them absent
Understanding autism in education: Teacher's opinions, student's lives
abstract: Abstract With autism diagnoses on the rise, autistic pupils are increasingly navigating mainstream education without adequate support, while class teachers bear responsibility for well‐being without proper training. Semi‐structured interviews were conducted with primary school teachers ( N = 5) to understand experiences of working with autistic pupils (AP). These findings were presented to a focus group of Autistic Students (AS) ( N = 7), reflecting on experiences of primary school in the UK. Both samples, through thematic analysis, identified preventative systemic barriers for inclusive education. AS were more action‐oriented in deconstructing systems; teachers focused more on developing practice for their specific classroom. Findings highlight the need for more training on autism inclusivity and more resources to implement accommodations.

title: Understanding complexity: Insights from Seashell's sector‐wide survey on education provision for young people with complex learning disabilities
abstract: Abstract This article shares findings from Seashell's 2024 complex needs survey, which aimed to address the critical lack of reliable cross‐sector data on children and young adults with learning disabilities and complex needs in England. The absence of consistent definitions and data collection methods across education, health and social care has long hindered inclusive strategic planning at local, regional and national levels. This project gathered data from 18 specialist providers through a national survey. Findings reveal that approximately 1800 children and young adults with learning disabilities and complex needs are currently educated by these providers, with autism spectrum condition and severe learning difficulty being the most reported primary needs. Respondents also reported a marked increase in the complexity of needs among their cohort, particularly in health and behavioural challenges, placing growing demands on specialist environments and staff. In response, some providers are expanding their capacity, with projected increases of 15.67% in education placements and 25.21% in residential placements. These findings align with national trends, including a rise in Educatio

title: Elevating ELT pedagogy: Bridging teacher training gaps for inclusive support of specific language learner difficulties
abstract: Abstract This research examines how scholars in English Language Teaching (ELT) and Special Education (SE) perceive and tackle Specific Language Learner Difficulties (SLLDs) in teacher education in Turkiye and existing pedagogical deficiencies. It suggests a paradigm for enhancing inclusive ELT methods in global educational settings. The research employed a qualitative methodology. Data were gathered through semi‐structured interviews with 10 academics chosen by purposive sampling. The interviews were thematically analysed, supported by MAXQDA. Research indicated conceptual ambiguity regarding SLLDs among ELT scholars, a lack of diagnostic awareness and inadequate differentiation in instruction and evaluation for learners with language‐based challenges. Collaboration between ELT and SE was informal and uneven; despite participants acknowledging the need for assistive technologies, their incorporation into ELT programmes was limited. The findings also underscored an absence of curriculum rules and institutional frameworks to facilitate inclusive ELT.

title: The impact of introducing relational approaches into four primary schools
abstract: Abstract In this two‐year project, four participating primary schools received training, support and investment to develop relational approaches and nurturing practices in their settings. The investment included funding for a nurture group, training for the nurture group staff and whole‐school staff training in attachment theory, neuroscience and emotion coaching. The socio‐emotional progress of 57 pupils attending a nurture group intervention was measured using the Boxall Profile® assessment instrument and staff focus group interviews reflected on any perceived changes to school ethos and practice over the course of the project. The impact of relational approaches on school suspension data was also investigated. The socio‐emotional progress made by pupils attending the nurture group intervention was found to be statistically significant and this progress was confirmed by qualitative observations made by staff. The development of relational approaches in school changed the way that adults spoke to children and to each other; schools felt calmer and more nurturing; and staff well‐being also improved. The impact on school suspension data was inconclusive. The findings recommend an in

title: School‐related needs of inclusion and multiple disabilities students via drawing analysis
abstract: Abstract Students in inclusive education experience problems due to insufficient support services, while those with multiple disabilities face challenges due to their complex needs. This study aimed to identify the unmet school‐related needs of both groups through an analysis of their drawings. The qualitative case study included 17 students aged 8–12 years, including 10 students with multiple disabilities enrolled in special education classrooms and 7 students receiving inclusive education. Data were collected through a General Information Form, ‘My Dream School’ drawings, and interviews, and analysed using a 12‐criteria list. Students with multiple disabilities emphasized emotional security, structured environments, and family connections in their artwork. Students in inclusive settings showed stronger school belonging and social awareness, and depicted functional school spaces. Drawings by students with multiple disabilities showed developmental stages below their chronological age, while students in inclusive education's drawings were age‐appropriate with greater control. Drawing analysis has proven effective for understanding the emotional, social, and physical needs of studen

title: Empowering teachers through community: Enhancing SEND practice across cultures
abstract: Abstract SEND Champions play an increasingly important role in supporting inclusive practice by acting as intermediaries between policy, professional learning and classroom implementation. While much research has explored inclusive pedagogy and teacher professional development, limited attention has been given to the specific experiences and support needs of SEND Champions, particularly within international and decentralised educational contexts. This practitioner research study explores how SEND Champions can be better supported in their roles and professional development in order to strengthen inclusive practice for learners with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND). Using a mixed‐methods survey distributed across an international SEND network, the study investigates their role demands, professional development experiences and the types of support most frequently sought by teachers. Findings indicate that SEND Champions face challenges related to time allocation, confidence in supporting neurodivergent learners and inconsistent systems for recording and reviewing SEND support. The study highlights the value of structured professional development and focused Communiti

title: Toward inclusion revisited: Inclusion as system work in the Australian context
abstract: Abstract This paper revisits ‘Towards Inclusion: An Australian Perspective’, published nearly two decades ago in Support for Learning . It offers a literature‐engaged, practice‐informed analysis of inclusive education in Australia. Drawing on sustained leadership experience across school, national, and international contexts, the paper concludes that inclusion is best understood as ongoing system work rather than a completed ‘reform’. It examines leadership of inclusion, systems coherence, teacher expertise and professional learning, and a long‐standing school‐based model of inclusive practice that demonstrates how specialist and mainstream expertise can operate collaboratively to enhance outcomes for learners. The paper positions the model as inclusion in action, offering a concrete example of how coherence can be co‐constructed within a federated education system.

title: The doubled‐edged sword of applying the Equality Act (2010) to dyslexia
abstract: Abstract This paper provided new theoretical insight into the pertinent benefits and limitations of applying the UK Equality Act (2010) in relation to dyslexia. The analysis captures a dichotomy in framing and interpreting dyslexia. Moreover, if dyslexia is conceptualised as a disability, access to legal protection, reasonable adjustments, and educational provision can be sought. However, by aligning dyslexia in this way, as a medical or educational need, this catalyses ableist narratives. In the wake of this, concepts of normalisation and standardised ways of operating can fortify structural hierarchies of normativity. Moreover, the paradox of disability classification impacts self‐efficacy; how individuals negotiate whether or not to disclose they have dyslexia. In the final analysis, this paper argued for clearer policy guidance and effective support without reinforcing stigma or marginalisation.

title: Exploring education practitioners' experiences and perceptions of using intensive interaction to support nonspeaking children who are educated in specialist settings
abstract: Abstract Nonspeaking children often face significant barriers to communication and inclusion in education. Intensive Interaction (II) is a relational, child‐led approach that supports early communication and social engagement through responsive, enjoyable, non‐goal‐oriented interactions. Drawing on semi‐structured interviews with five education practitioners, this qualitative study examines how II is implemented, the challenges practitioners face and its perceived impact on nonspeaking children. Reflexive Thematic Analysis generated four themes: (1) Following Children's Lead: The Art of Attuned Interaction, (2) Relational Foundations for Communication and Learning, (3) Supportive Ethos and Practice Normalise Vulnerability and Promote Professional Development and (4) Reframing the Meaning of Progress. Practitioners described II as an emotionally attuned process grounded in close observation and trust. Reported impacts included increased engagement, emotional regulation and deeper relational connection. Challenges included staffing pressures, institutional constraints and emotional vulnerability. Effective implementation depended on whole‐school cultures that legitimised relational w

title: Issue information
Beyond the surface: A critical analysis of superficial differentiation and the pursuit of purposeful and meaningful inclusion in mainstream schools
abstract: Abstract Inclusion within mainstream education is widely promoted with optimism, yet its enactment frequently falls short of its intent. While many schools adopt differentiated instruction to support diverse learners, such approaches can become superficial, focusing on cosmetic adjustments rather than deep, systemic change. This article critically examines the gap between superficial differentiation and purposeful, meaningful inclusion in school settings. Drawing on theoretical foundations such as Universal Design for Learning and Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory, the article argues that inclusion must move beyond technical accommodations to embrace a holistic approach that values student identity, agency and authentic participation. It highlights common practices that inadvertently reinforce exclusion under the guise of inclusion, including over‐reliance on generic accommodations and reactive interventions. The discussion identifies key principles underpinning meaningful inclusion, including collaborative planning, responsive curricula and leadership that prioritises equity and shared responsibility, while also examining persistent challenges such as limited professional learning,

title: Neurodiversity in storybooks and preschool inclusion: Findings on peer attitudes
abstract: Abstract Children's books are powerful educational tools that play a significant role in shaping values, attitudes and social understanding from an early age. Storybooks that address neurodiversity help children recognise differences as natural and acceptable while supporting the development of empathy and social acceptance. This study aims to examine the effects of storybooks used in inclusive preschool settings on neurotypical children's attitudes toward their neurodivergent peers and on how these books represent neurodiversity. A mixed‐methods approach, combining qualitative (document analysis and teacher interview) and quantitative (pre‐test and post‐test) data collection methods, has been used. The study involved 10 neurotypical children, one neurodivergent child and one preschool teacher, who were selected through purposive sampling. Data collection tools include a storybook analysis form, attitude scales and a teacher interview form. Findings suggest that storybooks featuring neurodiversity may contribute to more positive attitudes among neurotypical preschoolers toward their peers with neurodivergent development. While these initial results are promising, further research w

title: Describing the impact of an accessible literacy programme for children with profound and multiple learning difficulties on teaching staff
abstract: Abstract There is growing recognition of the visual learning needs of children with profound and multiple learning disabilities (PMLD). Dedicated training in visual impairment is lacking in teaching curricula. A literacy programme designed for PMLD children has been demonstrated to show benefits for this group of learners. The aim of this study was to understand the impact of the programme on teachers' confidence, understanding and practice when delivering visual learning for children with complex needs. An interview‐based qualitative study was undertaken with educators who have experience with the literacy programme. Data were analysed using thematic analysis. The results demonstrated that teachers themselves experience joy at the impact they are observing in pupils; they describe a deeper understanding of the visual needs of individuals and how to adapt the environment to extend this beyond the duration of the show. Programme users also express an improvement in confidence in how to produce accessible and inclusive materials and the courage to share this with peers to widen the knowledge base. An accessible literacy programme can demonstrate broader benefits beyond being a teachi

title: Are teachers aware of summer learning loss in students with SEND ? Cross‐sectional research
abstract: Abstract The purpose of the current research was to investigate teachers' knowledge, skills and perceptions about summer learning loss in students with Special Educational Needs and Disorders (SEND). The research employed a cross‐sectional survey model to investigate teachers' perceptions about summer learning loss in these students. It recruited teachers ( n = 251) working in K‐12 schools in the central region of Turkey. The research used a self‐administrated online data collection instrument within the survey methodology. The analysis was conducted on the dataset, utilising the frequencies ( f ) and percentages (%) to derive meaningful insights. The results suggested that teachers are aware of the main difficulties and challenges they encounter regarding learning loss amongst students with SEND during the summer months. However, most of them agree that they have limited knowledge about summer learning loss in those students.

title: Dyslexic students' relationships in mainstream classrooms: A cultural‐historical activity theory perspective
abstract: Abstract This multi‐temporal qualitative case study investigates how secondary school students with dyslexia understand and navigate their educational experiences and relationships in mainstream settings. Grounded in socio‐cultural and bio‐psycho‐social perspectives and analysed through cultural‐historical activity theory, the study explores how interactions among teachers, students and classroom tools shape inclusive practice. Eighteen participants—secondary students, university students reflecting on prior schooling and educators—took part in semi‐structured interviews and focus groups. Thematic analysis identified three overarching categories: structures, relationships and identity, with the current article focusing on relational experiences. Findings indicate that teacher understanding of dyslexia is central to students' sense of inclusion, confidence and academic engagement. Supportive relationships promoted coping, self‐advocacy and participation. The study highlights the need for improved dyslexia‐specific teacher training and relationally informed pedagogy. This lack of awareness can result in student disengagement, reduced self‐esteem and emotional distress.

title: Gamification in language learning for students with SEND : Mapping emerging evidence and implications for inclusive practice
abstract: Abstract Inclusive education policies increasingly emphasise equitable learning opportunities for pupils with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). At the same time, gamification has gained growing attention as a pedagogical approach intended to enhance learner engagement in language education. However, relatively little is known about how gamified learning environments function for learners with SEND. This review maps emerging evidence and identifies key gaps in research on gamification in SEND language learning contexts. A structured literature search was conducted across Scopus, Education Resources Information Center (ERIC) and Google Scholar, covering peer‐reviewed publications published between 2015 and 2025. Study selection followed PRISMA‐informed procedures, and four studies met the inclusion criteria and were analysed using a narrative synthesis approach. The findings provide preliminary evidence that gamified learning environments may support learner engagement, vocabulary development and aspects of reading performance. However, the evidence base remains limited and heterogeneous. In some cases, structured non‐gamified instruction demonstrated stronger outcom

title: Hear My Story: Educational psychologists' experiences of a multi‐sensory participatory approach to pupil voice for children with SEND
abstract: Abstract This article presents the findings from a qualitative study of Educational Psychologists' (EPs') experiences of implementing Hear My Story, a multi‐sensory data collection tool, developed to support children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) with communicating their lived experiences of education. Building upon phase 1 of this project, this second‐phase study explores the ways in which a group of EPs based in Northeast England facilitated, explored, and shared children's stories to support their experiences across education and health. The data analysed in this study were gathered via a focus group method, conducted after practitioners piloted the approach across mainstream and specialist settings. Thematic analysis generated four interrelated themes: (1) authenticity, enjoyment and emotional value; (2) facilitation and professional judgement; (3) accessibility; and (4) opportunities for embedding stories in practice. The findings indicate that Hear My Story provides a mechanism for surfacing nuanced insights into children's school experiences, and indeed, their experiences outside of school that influence their access to education. The article discuss

title: Correction to ‘Margins within the margins: The everyday realities of SC / ST students with disabilities in Kolkata's government and government‐aided schools’
Exploring professional development of special education teachers: A mixed‐method study on challenges and future needs
abstract: Abstract The professional development (PD) of special education teachers (SETs) in Pakistan is crucial for ensuring special education and addressing the diverse learning needs of students with disabilities. While global research highlights the effectiveness of disability‐specific modules, practical workshops and sustained mentoring, Pakistan continues to face systemic challenges, including insufficient resources, limited specialised training opportunities, weak career advancement pathways and minimal cross‐cultural exposure. This study aimed to assess the challenges in PD programmes for SETs and to identify future needs for improvement. A mixed‐methods convergent parallel design was employed, combining quantitative and qualitative approaches. Data were collected through a validated structured questionnaire administered to 390 SETs across Punjab (Cronbach's α = 0.974) and through semi‐structured interviews with 20 stakeholders, continued until data saturation was achieved, including trainers, institutional heads and programme directors, selected using multistage sampling. The findings revealed significant systemic gaps, such as the predominance of generic rather than disability‐spec

title: Experiences of student teachers with visual impairments on teaching practice (internship) at Colleges of Education in Ghana
abstract: Abstract This study explored the experiences of student teachers with visual impairment during teaching practice (internship) in Colleges of Education in Ghana. Grounded in the social model of disability, it examined the nature of support provided by colleges, schools of practice, mentors and peers, as well as the challenges encountered. A phenomenological design was adopted, involving eight Level 400 student teachers with visual impairment from three Colleges of Education. Data were collected through semi‐structured interviews and analysed thematically. Findings revealed that although institutional structures such as orientation and supervision exist, they are largely generic and insufficiently responsive to disability‐specific needs. Support from mentors and schools was inconsistent, while peer support emerged as a critical yet informal mechanism facilitating mobility, lesson preparation and instructional delivery. Participants experienced significant challenges, including physical inaccessibility, limited assistive resources, inadequate mentoring and negative attitudes from some learners and teachers. The study concludes that teaching practice remains inadequately inclusive and

title: The support needs of student teachers from an accessibility perspective
abstract: Abstract We studied what kind of support needs student teachers have in higher education. A total of 769 student teachers responded to a questionnaire in 2018 and 2022, and 90 of them specified their support needs during their higher education. The most common needs were related to pedagogical and psychological accessibility: students hoped for versatile teaching methods and encouragement from teachers. The results indicate that teacher education should focus on accessibility and support to ensure that all students receive the support they need and are included.

title: Claiming freedom: Sexual autonomy and the rights of adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities in India
abstract: Abstract Despite protections under India's Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act (2016) and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) continue to face barriers to sexual autonomy and inclusive learning. Although UNCRPD Article 24 mandates inclusive education at all levels, sexuality education for individuals with IDD remains marginal within school curricula, transition planning and adult education systems. Using a mixed‐perspective qualitative design, this study draws on surveys from 85 professionals, caregivers and advocates, alongside interviews with 24 self‐advocates in urban Mumbai. Thematic analysis identified structural, institutional and caregiver‐mediated barriers alongside themes reflecting self‐advocate agency. Findings highlight curriculum gaps, cultural stigma and policy ambiguity across school‐to‐adult transitions and community learning contexts. We call for a rights‐based sexuality education framework spanning school and adult education, supported by educator training, caregiver engagement and policy reform to strengthen autonomy and inclusive participation.

title: Supporting students with ADHD : Teachers' self‐reported knowledge of ADHD in planning and implementing strategies for social and emotional wellbeing
abstract: Abstract Children and young people with attention‐deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) experience not only variations to executive functioning, but also an increased risk of experiencing poor mental health. Despite the acknowledgement of this increased risk, previous studies suggest that school‐based support for students with ADHD prioritises their academic needs over their social–emotional wellbeing. This study explores how teachers' self‐reported knowledge of ADHD affects the strategies they employ to support students' social–emotional wellbeing. A qualitative survey was conducted with 12 teachers in Australia and data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The results show that although teachers perceived they had substantial knowledge of ADHD, this knowledge did not consistently translate into support for students' social and emotional wellbeing (SEW). Instead, SEW support was limited and shaped more strongly by external constraints such as workload, insufficient training, and parent collaboration challenges.

title: Margins within the margins: The everyday realities of SC / ST students with disabilities in Kolkata's government and government‐aided schools
abstract: Abstract This study examines the experiences of Scheduled Caste (SC) and Scheduled Tribe (ST) students with disabilities in government schools in Kolkata, India, exploring how the intersection of caste and disability influences access to inclusive education. Using qualitative methods, including classroom observations and interviews with students, teachers and community members, the research highlights a spectrum of practices and conditions. It identifies promising inclusive strategies such as peer support, teacher sensitivity and informal differentiation, while also drawing attention to persistent challenges, including large class sizes, limited teacher preparation and caste‐related social dynamics. The children's voices offer insight into the emotional and relational aspects of school life, revealing moments of belonging as well as subtle exclusions. The study advocates for intersectionally informed teacher development, stronger community‐school linkages and culturally responsive approaches that can be adapted to low‐resource settings. Implications are offered for educators, school leaders and policymakers working toward equitable and inclusive education.

title: Lost in translation: The role of English as a barrier in autism support for multilingual children in Bangalore, India
abstract: Abstract This paper explores the role of English as a linguistic barrier in the education and therapy of children in the early years with autism in Bangalore, South India, a region marked by rich multilingualism. Despite the linguistic diversity of its population, most special education and therapeutic interventions in Bangalore are delivered primarily in English. Drawing on over a decade of field experience from practitioner journals, parental narratives and case reflections, this study uses a narrative inquiry methodology to highlight the ways in which English‐only environments limit access, understanding and emotional engagement for these children. It further identifies how mothers, who are often primary caregivers, struggle to engage in therapeutic processes due to limited English proficiency, leading to decreased continuity and effectiveness of intervention at home. Findings point to the systemic exclusion that occurs when English is the default medium in inclusive education and therapy, often misinterpreting language‐related confusion or distress as behavioural issues. This paper calls for a redefinition of inclusion that embraces linguistic diversity and recommends multiling

title: School‐based induction for newly qualified teachers in classroom and special education teaching roles: How school‐based induction supports inclusive and special education teaching practices
abstract: Abstract This article explores how school‐based induction supported Newly Qualified Teachers (NQTs) to develop inclusive teaching practices in a mainstream primary school in Ireland. Focusing on an NQT in a mainstream class and an NQT in a Special Education Teacher (SET) role, the study examines how structured reflective dialogue, collaborative mentoring and leadership shaped their confidence and practice. Using a qualitative case study design, data were gathered from semistructured interviews, weekly reflective meetings and researcher field notes. Findings show that protected reflective space, intentional SET–mainstream collaboration with mentors who engaged in dialogic, non‐evaluative support enabled NQTs to move beyond ‘survival mode’ toward inclusive pedagogical decision‐making. However, access to collaborative learning varied by teacher role, highlighting the need for equitable induction structures. The study contributes to current Irish policy debates by highlighting that school‐based induction can embed inclusive practice when reflective learning is prioritised, SETs are positioned as co‐educators, and leadership protects time and role clarity.

title: Autistic and Black: Our experiences of growth, progress and empowerment By Kala AllenOmeiza, London and Philidelphia: Jessica Kingsley Publishers. 2024. ISBN: 9781839976209
Inclusion and collaboration: What do trainee educational psychologists in Ireland think?
abstract: Abstract Inclusive education is a central topic in the field of education, fuelled by national and international policy and legislation. While there is no universally accepted definition of inclusive education in Ireland or elsewhere, it is widely recognised that collaboration among relevant stakeholders is a core principle underpinning inclusive practice. This paper explores Irish trainee educational psychologists' (TEPs) understanding of inclusive education, with a particular focus on the importance of meaningful collaboration with school staff and parents. A qualitative study was conducted with 33 TEPs, including 12 semi‐structured interviews and 21 responses to an online qualitative questionnaire. Five broad themes were constructed from the research; one of which will be discussed in this paper. Reflexive Thematic Analysis (RTA) identified five overarching themes, one of which—‘collaboration’—is the focus of the current article. As part of this theme, the discussion is structured around three sub‐themes: building ongoing school‐wide practices, fostering an inclusive school culture and respecting parental choice. The findings highlight the critical role of collaborative relation

title: A case study on the efficacy of identifying the learning style of children with autism using Dunn and Dunn's model to design differentiated lessons
abstract: Abstract The small‐scale case study reported here investigated the efficacy of the Dunn and Dunn learning style model and its relationship to learners with Autism. This qualitative study was conducted in a special school in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India. The aim was to provide support to teachers to design and deliver more effective lessons. Twenty special educators from this special school were provided with questionnaires containing open and closed‐ended questions. All twenty special educators were of the view that identifying and recording the learning style using the Dunn and Dunn model in children with Autism helped in preparing effective differentiated lessons.

title: ‘Square pegs, round holes’—A qualitative case study investigating pupils with attention‐deficit hyperactivity disorder and their perception of barriers to inclusion in classrooms in the north of England
abstract: Abstract Attention‐deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a commonly diagnosed disorder in children and young people. The majority of research focuses on a biomedical management model of the disorder, aiming to limit the impact of symptoms and behaviour typically associated with the disorder. Quantitative research has typically been used to investigate ADHD, with studies failing to take into account the voice of young people. A significant proportion of research has taken place in America and the South of England. Research with young people in the North of England is limited. Recent research focusing specifically on educational experiences is also limited. This study aimed to present the views and experiences of young people with ADHD through a qualitative approach, specifically focusing on their experiences in education. This study contributes to current literature by voicing the experiences of young people in the North of England. Six participants took part in a qualitative study answering questions in a semi‐structured interview. Qualitative methods were employed to enable the voice of participants to be fully heard and presented in the research. Reflexive thematic analysis wa

title: Reducing mental distress and promoting positive mental well‐being in autistic girls who camouflage
abstract: Abstract The psychological well‐being of autistic pupils is often worse compared to that of their neurotypical peers, with evidence suggesting that autistic girls are in an even worse position. We argue that this is due to traits of the autistic female phenotype, including the phenomenon of social camouflaging which is motivated by the human need for belonging. Camouflaging has a dual role in exacerbating outcomes for autistic girls at school; first, it prevents identification of their needs, and second, it can contribute to mental distress. As autistic girls are more likely to engage in camouflaging, and because they have an increased likelihood of mental distress compared to autistic boys, it is important for school professionals to be aware of the strategies of compensation, masking and assimilation that these girls are likely to employ and to work towards eliminating their need to camouflage, through identifying and working with their strengths and, therefore, promoting true social inclusion at school.

title: The role of dance in supporting social inclusion and skill development for children experiencing complex needs
abstract: Abstract This article examines how dance has been used to help children experiencing complex needs (CECN) improve their social skills and encourage inclusion within local communities. Building on initial research conducted in India where I trained as a dancer and completed my MA work in a school for children with special educational needs (SEN), this study reflects a continued commitment to exploring the role of dance in inclusive education. The current research, conducted in two UK schools, involved teaching dance to groups of CECN alongside participant observation through video recordings of the lessons. Interviews with pupils, parents and teachers further informed the study. The research aimed to address four main questions regarding the benefits of dance, particularly in enhancing social interactions and promoting inclusion. Findings reveal that dance plays a crucial role in improving communication, self‐confidence and social integration for CECN. The study provides encouraging results and highlights the potential of dance as an effective tool for inclusion and social development, suggesting that further research is needed to explore its full potential and application in educat

title: A place for all: Trends in special and inclusive education in India
abstract: Abstract Education is the fundamental Right of every citizen of India. To exercise that right is a challenge when the person has a disability. The education of individuals with disabilities has come a long way in India, ranging from total rejection by schools, to right based education. Getting to know the educational system in India since BCE to current practices leads to understanding the socio‐cultural ethos that impact the principles of ‘education for all’ in India. This narrative study with specific focus on current trends, practices and challenges was carried out through a review of government publications and documents, research studies and other relevant literature. The impact of international mandates and national policies on the educational systems are highlighted. In addition, the diverse socio‐cultural, linguistic economic and geographical factors that influence the educational system and the efforts taken by the various Boards of Education at Central and State levels are discussed. Findings reveal that in essence, the policy of inclusive education espoused by the ministry of education reaches a large number of children in regular schools throughout the country, while th

title: Coastal pedagogy as a framework for inclusive education: Reimagining practice in India through a village‐based intervention in the Trivandrum district of Kerala
abstract: Abstract This paper explores an ocean arts project aimed at enhancing the learning outcomes of the Mukkuvar—coastal community children in India, where inclusive education often overlooks cultural and linguistic diversity. By integrating Indigenous and Local Knowledge with scientific knowledge, the project created culturally relevant curriculum materials and involved community members—especially fathers/fishermen—in the learning process. Implemented during school holidays, the programme improved student engagement and academic outcomes. Using a mixed method, the study shows the value of unique community skills as a medium for new learning. Findings suggest mainstream education should embrace such community knowledge and skills to support culturally responsive pedagogy.
